newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEPs to adopt new rules of conduct for lobbyists.
newsitem.headline: MEPs to adopt new rules of conduct for lobbyists.

text.p: The European Parliament is due next Tuesday to approve a code of conduct for the estimated 3,000 lobbyists vying for Euro-MPs' attention.

The draft code, proposed by British Socialist Glyn Ford, obliges lobbyists to tell Euro-MPs of the interest groups they represent and present parliament with an annual report on their lobbying activities.
It also bans lobbyists from claiming to third parties that they have an official relationship with parliament and from selling parliamentary documents to other people.
Any lobbyists found breaking these rules or trying to obtain information dishonestly will be refused an entry pass to the parliament's buildings in Brussels and Strasbourg.
The activities of Euro-MPs' assistants will also be controlled more tightly in future.

A number of Euro-MPs, including Ford, have complained that some assistants, who have free access to parliament's meetings and telephone lines to the four corners of the world, are actually working as lobbyists.
The new code of conduct says only registered assistants, who work exclusively for Euro-MPs, will have free access to the parliament in future.

Last July, Euro-MPs approved hotly disputed rules on Euro-MPs' conduct which said deputies could continue legitimately to accept gifts from industries and lobbies but only so long as they publicly declared them.
Undeclared gifts or donations are now banned but there are no sanctions for MEPs who fail to reveal what they receive, other than public condemnation if they are found out.

The newly created Society of European Affairs Practitioners (SEAP, which represents the interests of the lobbying industry, said on Wednesday it welcomed the code of conduct in principle but was concerned about the possible implications.

"We will...be taking interest in the detail of the parliament code to ensure that we are able to carry out our own work in the most effective and transparent way, to enable third parties to participate in the political consulation process," SEAP chairman Richard Chorus said in a statement.
